title: Does Laughter Matter? Isolating the Effects of Laughter in Laughter Yoga: A Randomized Controlled Trial
summary:
Laughter yoga combines different exercises, including intentional or simulated laughter, breathing exercises, clapping and playful movements. There is some evidence that laughter yoga may promote physical and psychological well-being. However, it is still unclear how much of these effects can specifically be attributed to laughter itself.
The aim of this study is therefore to investigate the specific effects of laughter within laughter yoga on physical, psychological and social experiences.
A total of 100 adults aged 18 years or older will take part in the study. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. Both groups will take part in an approximately 30-minute group session with 10–15 participants, led by two trained laughter yoga instructors.
The intervention group will take part in a standard laughter yoga session including simulated laughter, breathing exercises, clapping and playful movements. The control group will perform the same exercises for a similar amount of time and in the same format, but without simulated laughter. This allows us to investigate the specific contribution of laughter itself.
Before and after the session, participants will complete questionnaires about their 
their experiences with the other people in the group, their current mood, stress, and well-being. Heart rate and the hormone oxytocin in saliva will also be measured. Any adverse events occurring during the study will be recorded.
The study will take place as part of the “Long Night of Sciences” at Jena University Hospital. The results may help to better understand the effects of laughter yoga and, in particular, the role of laughter itself.
conditions: Healthy participants experiencing mild to severe stress

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Fluent in German language
Exclusion criteria:
Any type of visceral hernia or inguinal hernia
Untreated high blood pressure, aneurysms or heart conditions involving angina pectoris
Recent surgery (within the last 3 months) or acute pain
Persistent cough with shortness of breath or severe asthma
Urinary incontinence
Epilepsy
Pregnancy and the postnatal period (<8 weeks)
Severe mental health conditions
Having a pacemaker or other medical implants
Disease or dysfunction of the pituitary gland, hypothalamus or adrenal glands (e.g. tumours or Cushing’s syndrome)
(self-reported symptoms/conditions in each case)
